_doc: The engine's looks: what a game made 'for a console' means, as data. Read by tools/looks.py (the phrase -> look table), tools/look_check.py (the checker) and tools/new_game.py --look. Prose rules stay in docs/art.md ('Choose a look'); the numbers here are the ones that can be checked. limits: pal_bank_colours = most colours in a 16-entry bank of a .pal (index 0 is see-through); image_bpp / image_colours = most for a packed picture; sprite = largest frame; pictures = false means no picture assets at all.

looks.name: Game Boy
looks.era: 1998 · four greens, a world of screens
looks.world: 240x160 (status bar on top, level under it)
looks.style: Game Boy pixel art, four shades of green, 8x8 tiles, no anti-aliasing
rules: four tones, lightest to darkest, written into WORLD.pal / OBJ.pal before converting so pal() recolours the whole game
8x8 tiles in one background layer, 16x16 sprites, a status bar and dialogue as a window layer
two square voices and a noise; music as 4-channel .mod or tone()
avoid: drawing a 160x144 console case around the screen (wastes a third of it) unless asked
more than four tones in a bank

looks.name: ZX Spectrum
looks.style: ZX Spectrum pixel art, two colours per 8x8 block, bright and normal, colour clash
rules: an ink and a paper per 8x8 block from the fifteen colours; blocks drawn in two key colours, coloured by a palette bank per block
sprites are ink only and take the bank of the block they stand in (the colour clash)
one square voice (the beeper)
avoid: a third colour inside a block

looks.name: PICO-8
looks.world: 128x128 in the middle of the 240x160 world
looks.style: PICO-8 pixel art, the sixteen fixed colours, 8x8 sprites
rules: the sixteen PICO-8 colours and no others, at palette indices 1-16
a 16x16 map of 8x8 tiles, pal() for fades
four chiptune channels with tone()

looks.name: Pocket LCD
looks.world: the handheld's plate, glass drawn once
looks.style: pocket LCD game: fixed figures on or off over a printed picture
rules: every figure is a fixed shape, on (dark) or off (a faint ghost); all polygons
the glass is drawn once and kept as one picture, only what is on is drawn each frame
steps with a beep, faster as the score grows; seven-segment score, games A and B
avoid: a full-screen 480x320 canvas for the glass (about 100 ms a frame on the console)

looks.name: Vector arcade
looks.style: vector arcade: bright lines on black with a soft glow
rules: no pictures at all: poly/line only
an outline is ONE poly() call (cost is by call, not by pixel); keep strokes in a list and draw every glow, then every core
letters made of strokes
avoid: a glow picture under the lines (4-5 ms a frame)

looks.name: Game Boy Advance
looks.style: 16-bit handheld pixel art, 4 to 8 colours per sprite, hard pixel edges, no anti-aliasing
rules: characters 16 to 32 px, 8x8 tiles in sixteen-colour banks, 128 sprites
a full-screen layer costs about a fifth of a frame on the console: paint sky + hills into one picture and scroll it with line_scroll
blend, window+fade and whole-screen ripples cost a third to two thirds of a frame each: use them on part of the screen
avoid: four full layers (the first Botín ran at 30 fps)
more than 15 colours in a bank

looks.name: Super Nintendo · Mega Drive
looks.style: 16-bit console pixel art, 15 colours per sprite, bold outlines, saturated colours, no anti-aliasing
rules: sprites up to 32x32 (bigger in a few), 15 colours each or fewer
Mega Drive: far layers at a different speed per line (line_scroll); SNES: line_backdrop sky, blend water, mosaic between scenes, Mode 7 floors

looks.name: PlayStation · Saturn 2D
looks.style: late-1990s 32-bit console 2D sprite art, up to 256 colours, smooth careful shading, crisp pixel edges
rules: characters about 90 px in up to 256 colours
light and transparency: img add / alpha for glows and ghosts, only on what moves (a mixed pixel costs about three plain ones)
a picture drawn by quad() should be 128x128 or less; dither = true gives the PlayStation's pattern
sounds as ADPCM and a reverb room for the whole soundtrack
avoid: a quad texture bigger than 128x128 (six times the cost)

looks.name: Neo Geo
looks.style: mid-1990s Neo Geo sprite art, painterly, 3 to 4 tones per material, hard pixel edges, no anti-aliasing
rules: every pixel at 480x320 with img() of packed pictures; characters 90 to 180 px
sheets in pieces of ten frames (tools/pk_split.py) so the console never needs one big block
hand-animated frames in quantity, comic deaths; sprites can only be shrunk, never grown
one reference image per character, then one sheet per move (docs/art.md section 2); fit scale and baseline in code
avoid: code-drawn characters next to painted backgrounds (Paella's first version looked flat)
one big picture per sheet (PSRAM fragments)

looks.name: CPS2
looks.style: mid-1990s 2D arcade fighting game sprite, hand-pixelled, bold dark outline, cel shading with 3 or 4 tones per material, about 15 colours in total
rules: characters 125 to 140 px in 15 colours and see-through (--colours 16, four bits a pixel)
no zoom: everyone keeps the size they were drawn at, the camera only pans
a floor in perspective drawn in bands of rows, pillars in front, the same character in other colours with pal()
avoid: more than 15 colours in a character

looks.name: Vertical arcade
looks.style: vertical arcade shooter, bright sprites on a dark scrolling field
rules: draw on a 320x480 canvas standing up, shown with img(..., {angle = 90}); the console is held on its side
read the arrows turned the same way
hundreds of bullets as swarms
avoid: forgetting that the player holds the console on its side

looks.name: First person
looks.world: 240x160 raycast canvas shown twice as big under a status bar
looks.style: early 1990s raycaster, 32x32 or 64x64 wall textures, 32x32 sprites in the maze
rules: raycast() onto a 240x160 canvas shown twice as big
walls are 32x32 (or 64x64) textures, sprites 32x32 pictures standing in the maze

nes: NES: use the Game Boy rules (8x8 tiles, banks of 4 colours = 3 + see-through) but the NES colours, a palette per bank
master system: 8-bit tiles and banks; 16 colours of a 64 palette
game gear: same as master system, a small screen
pc engine: tiles and sprites like the 16-bit looks, 512 colours; fewer colours per bank
